strengths: Addresses a well-motivated research question with practical relevance (pathwise gradients in on-policy RL without large replay buffers)
Extensive and rigorous experimental evaluation across 31 diverse tasks with multiple metrics (sample efficiency, wall-clock time, memory, stability) and proper statistical reporting
Strong empirical results: consistent improvements over PPO in sample efficiency and stability, competitive with FastTD3 while using 100-1000× smaller memory
Thoughtful algorithm design with novel joint entropy-KL tuning approach that is well-motivated and validated through ablations
Comprehensive ablation studies isolating contributions of HL-Gauss loss, layer normalization, auxiliary tasks, and KL regularization
Demonstrates high hyperparameter robustness with single hyperparameter set across 30+ tasks
Good presentation with clear motivation, pedagogical elements (gradient comparison), and detailed algorithm description
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: combines established techniques (TD(λ), maximum entropy RL, KL regularization, pathwise gradients) without significant new conceptual insights or theoretical contributions
Narrow evaluation domain: only GPU-parallelized simulation benchmarks tested, despite memory efficiency motivation being most relevant for non-parallelized settings; no real robot experiments

Evaluation concerns: different seed counts (10 vs 4-5 for baselines) affecting confidence intervals; unclear PPO baseline tuning effort relative to REPPO's extensive design; FastTD3 constrained buffer setup is artificial
No theoretical analysis of convergence, value function approximation error, or conditions for success/failure; lacks understanding of when method should work vs. fail
Incomplete reproducibility: code address referenced but missing; multiple 'Appendix ??' citations; hyperparameter choices (HL-Gauss bins=151, σ, λ=0.95) appear arbitrary without justification
Value function quality not directly measured (no MSE, distributional analysis) despite this being central to pathwise gradient quality

Architectural components incompletely analyzed: auxiliary task has inconsistent impact (beneficial in some tasks, harmful in others) without explanation; layer normalization retained despite being less critical

Wall-clock time analysis acknowledged as problematic (framework-dependent, compilation overhead) with results limited to single hardware setup; claims of 'on par with PPO' in wall-clock time are unreliable
Missing comparisons: no evaluation against other value-based on-policy methods, SAC in on-policy mode, or PQN; limited engagement with concurrent work on stabilizing pathwise gradients
Incomplete failure analysis: FingerSpin suboptimal convergence and PPO wins on some tasks are noted but not investigated; suboptimal solution in some environments suggests systematic weaknesses

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing on-policy pathwise gradient learning with practical memory benefits
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 31+ environments with multiple evaluation metrics (performance, sample efficiency, wall-clock time, memory, stability)
Rigorous experimental protocol with 10 random seeds and detailed ablation studies demonstrating component necessity
Practical advantages: orders of magnitude smaller memory footprint than off-policy methods while maintaining competitive performance
Clear presentation with reproducible implementation (code in JAX and PyTorch) and detailed hyperparameters
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (TD-λ, max entropy RL, KL constraints, DPG, HL-Gauss) without clear algorithmic or conceptual innovation beyond PQN for continuous actions
Unclear mechanistic understanding: no detailed analysis of why these specific components enable on-policy pathwise gradients or how Q-function quality compares to alternatives during training

Mixed and inconsistent empirical results: REPPO doesn't consistently outperform baselines (acknowledged failures on FingerSpin), many environments show overlapping confidence intervals, and performance varies across metrics (mean vs median vs IQM)

Questionable comparison methodology: PPO baselines appear potentially under-tuned with inconsistent tuning protocols; FastTD3 memory comparison artificially constrains buffer; no comparison with other recent on-policy methods beyond PPO

Ad-hoc architectural choices with unexplained necessity: auxiliary task explicitly harmful in some environments; components like HL-Gauss and layer normalization added without principled justification for on-policy setting

Hyperparameter robustness claim is overstated: despite claiming 'single hyperparameter set', paper reveals discount factor γ and HL-Gauss bounds are tuned per-environment, plus multiple other tunable components (α, β, learning rates, λ, auxiliary weight)
Limited scope: only continuous control with state observations; no discrete actions, pixels, or standard benchmarks like Atari; acknowledged struggles with sparse rewards and exploration
Weak wall-clock analysis: only JAX implementation compared; Appendix explicitly states framework differences 'dominate' and recommends against trusting wall-clock claims
Missing critical analyses: no ablation on maximum entropy component alone, no exploration behavior comparison, limited forward vs reverse KL analysis, no systematic TD(λ) ablation
Presentation gaps: missing implementation details referenced as '??'; claims like 'significantly faster' lack quantitative support given overlapping confidence intervals

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a genuine gap: using pathwise policy gradients effectively in on-policy RL with limited memory requirements
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 31 tasks across two benchmarks with multiple metrics (final performance, sample efficiency, wall-clock time, memory, policy stability)
Strong empirical results: outperforms PPO on aggregate metrics, competitive with FastTD3 while using 100-1000x less memory, demonstrates 80% reliable success rate vs 40% for PPO
Excellent reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, architectural specifications, clear algorithm pseudocode, code release promised in JAX and PyTorch
Thorough ablations (Figure 7) clearly demonstrate necessity of HL-Gauss loss and KL regularization across different data scales
Practical robustness: single hyperparameter set effective across 30+ diverse tasks with only environment-specific γ and HL-Gauss bin tuning
Clear pedagogical presentation: Figure 1 effectively illustrates importance of surrogate value quality, well-motivated design choices
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: combines existing components (TD-λ, maximum entropy RL, KL constraints, HL-Gauss loss, layer normalization). Joint entropy-KL tuning is the main novel element but relatively straightforward. Similar ideas in concurrent work (PQN)
Missing theoretical understanding: no convergence analysis, lack of formal justification for why this combination works, forward vs. reverse KL choice only empirically motivated
Inconsistent auxiliary loss component: acknowledged by authors as beneficial in some tasks but detrimental in others, questioning its necessity and reproducibility

Experimental scope limitations: only continuous control with GPU-parallel environments; no image observations (despite claimed advantage), discrete actions, or exploration of failure modes like FingerSpin

Contradiction between claims and implementation: claims 'single hyperparameter set' robustness but uses per-environment tuning of γ and HL-Gauss bins; different random seed counts (10 vs 4-5) for statistical comparison

Incomplete analysis: no Q-value quality metrics or error distribution analysis; limited investigation of when/why method succeeds or fails; baseline PPO could benefit from same architectural improvements
Wall-clock time results are framework-dependent with significant caveats (Appendix B); 33% speedup is modest; missing reference number in results section ('??')

Limited comparison to related work: distinguishes from PQN primarily on continuous action handling, but this distinction feels narrow; missing comparisons to other recent on-policy value-based methods

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 31+ environments with solid statistical rigor (20 seeds, bootstrapped confidence intervals)
Demonstrates effective combination of existing techniques to enable pathwise gradients in on-policy RL, with strong hyperparameter robustness across diverse tasks
Thorough ablation studies (Figure 10) clearly showing necessity of key components, and honest discussion of experimental limitations (wall-clock time challenges in Appendix A)
Clear problem motivation and well-specified algorithm (Algorithm 1) with implementations in both JAX and PyTorch for reproducibility
Practical advantages: no large replay buffers, orders of magnitude lower memory footprint than off-policy methods, consistent single hyperparameter set for most hyperparameters
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Core components (maximum entropy RL, KL constraints, TD-λ, HL-Gauss) are borrowed from existing work; primarily engineering contribution combining known techniques

Overclaimed experimental results: Wall-clock time comparison shows only ~33% higher return than PPO after equal time despite higher per-update cost; ManiSkill mean actually favors PPO (only IQM/median favor REPPO); DMC per-environment results mixed with PPO winning on several tasks; D-REPPO underperforms PQN on discrete tasks
Insufficient theoretical understanding: No convergence analysis or principled explanation for why biased Q-functions suffice; missing analysis of when/why on-policy targets avoid off-policy issues

Overstated hyperparameter robustness: While α, β, λ are fixed, γ, vmin, vmax are still auto-tuned per environment, contradicting 'single hyperparameter set' narrative; unclear if true fixed hyperparameters work

Fragile value function learning: Requires multiple stabilization components (HL-Gauss loss, layer norm, auxiliary task); auxiliary task has inconsistent effects (helpful in some environments, harmful in others) with no principled explanation

Experimental setup inconsistencies: FastTD3 evaluated with only 5 seeds vs 20 for REPPO; authors unable to replicate FastTD3's claimed speed; hyperparameter setup constraints for comparisons not fully justified
Scope limitations: Evaluation limited to GPU-parallelized environments and dense-reward settings; no real-world robot experiments; no image-based observations despite on-policy memory advantages

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 31+ tasks with proper statistical reporting (confidence intervals, multiple metrics)
Clear practical benefits: competitive performance with PPO while using significantly lower memory than off-policy methods
Strong empirical results on training stability (Figure 7: reliable success metric) showing fewer catastrophic failures
Thorough ablation studies (Figure 10) demonstrating the importance of individual components
Honest methodological discussion including wall-clock timing challenges and framework-specific considerations
Thoughtful design for on-policy learning: multi-step TD-λ targets with maximum entropy exploration and adaptive KL constraints
weaknesses: Limited core algorithmic novelty: primarily combines existing well-known techniques (maximum entropy RL since 2008, KL-constrained updates since 2010-2015, standard on-policy TD-λ) without sufficient new insight

Critical dependence on off-the-shelf architectural tricks (HL-Gauss loss, layer normalization, auxiliary tasks) borrowed from concurrent work—Figure 10 shows removing these significantly harms performance, suggesting the core algorithm lacks inherent robustness
Insufficient differentiation from concurrent work PQN (Gallici et al. 2024), which addresses the same problem; D-REPPO actually underperforms PQN on discrete tasks (2.98 vs 3.35)
Loose connection between theoretical formulation (constrained optimization Eqs. 10-12) and actual implementation (ad-hoc clipped objective Eq. 15); no convergence analysis or theoretical guarantees
Overclaimed hyperparameter robustness: Table 2 shows per-environment tuning of γ, vmin, vmax despite claims of 'single hyperparameter set'
Incomplete baseline comparisons: FastTD3 evaluated with only 5 seeds (vs 20 for REPPO), no direct SAC comparison, RPO/DPO couldn't exceed PPO despite tuning
Statistical significance concerns: ManiSkill results show very broad confidence intervals for REPPO; DMC mean comparisons have overlapping CIs; overclaimed significance given high variance
Auxiliary task design inconsistency: acknowledged to be 'crucial for learning' in some environments but harmful in others, indicating lack of robustness
Heavy reliance on architectural innovations from Farebrother et al. (2024), Hussing et al. (2024) makes the contribution feel more like 'combining tricks' than principled algorithmic advance

Missing analysis of Q-function quality: paper argues accurate value functions are critical but doesn't measure whether REPPO's Q-networks are actually better than baselines or remain accurate during training with only on-policy data

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 31+ diverse tasks with rigorous experimental methodology (multiple metrics, ablations, confidence intervals)

Solves a genuine practical problem: enables pathwise policy gradients in on-policy settings while avoiding large replay buffers, achieving 2-3 orders of magnitude memory savings vs. off-policy methods
Strong and consistent empirical results demonstrating improved sample efficiency, hyperparameter robustness (single hyperparameter set across 30+ tasks), and stable policy improvements (Figure 7)
Thorough presentation with detailed algorithm pseudocode, implementation details, ablation studies, and code in two frameworks—strong reproducibility
Clear technical approach thoughtfully combining maximum entropy exploration, KL constraints, and architectural components with well-motivated design choices
Honest discussion of limitations and experimental challenges (wall-clock time comparisons, framework-specific issues) showing research integrity
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (pathwise gradients, maximum entropy, KL constraints, HL-Gauss loss, layer normalization) rather than introducing fundamentally new concepts

Weak theoretical justification: no formal analysis of why on-policy value function learning provides sufficient quality for pathwise gradient estimation or why the approach avoids instability despite using biased surrogate values

KL constraint implementation (Equation 15) is ad-hoc and heuristic-based (hard switching between objectives), lacking principled theoretical grounding; why the alternative joint objective (Equation 16) underperforms is not analyzed

Overstated robustness claims: while claiming single hyperparameter set, γ and HL-Gauss parameters are tuned per environment (page 22); auxiliary tasks help some tasks but harm others (pages 8, 24), suggesting inconsistent benefits
Incomplete wall-clock time evaluation: only JAX comparison with PPO (Figure 6); FastTD3 excluded due to framework issues, limiting practical conclusions about speed-performance tradeoffs
Discrete action variant (D-REPPO) underperforms PQN on Atari-10 (mean 2.98 vs 3.35), and paper lacks investigation into why concurrent trust-region methods (RPO, DPO) fail while REPPO succeeds

Missing empirical characterization of value function quality: no analysis of Q-value errors during training or correlation between estimated/actual returns, which would strengthen on-policy feasibility claims
